I want to talk about some of the other books I've read over the years, and I'm going to add a brief line or two about what I took away from them.

I'll start with "Anthem" by Any Rand. This one was tricky to get into at first, because I didn't understand why a first person narrator wasn't using "I" or "me" at any point and kept saying "we" and "us". In this society recuperating from some sort of catastrophic event, our hero gets designated as a janitor for being too smart, and too willing to bring technology back to a deliberately enforced backwards age. Overall a short, decent read that's worth exploring in an afternoon.

"The Giver" by Lois Lowry. Fascinating one, recently converted to a movie (which I'll confess I haven't seen). In this, it's a society of average folks with no deviations across the board. The main character perceives the world in black and white, and in general there is a VERY homogeneous aspect to the book. Everyone is essentially the same except for the designated "Giver" who holds humanity's powerful memories. Memories of war, of happiness, sadness, anger, cold, starvation, greed, experiencing the miracle of childbirth, EVERYTHING. This was a largely emotionless society, by force and choice. Conceptually interesting at least, but difficult to fathom technology allowing the more fantastical elements of the story. Nevertheless, it's worth reading.

"Fahrenheit 451", the temp which books burn. Interestingly, one of the causes of the decline of society was too many special interest minorities demanding protection from the law, which gradually eroded the freedom of authors, comedians and the like to the point of irrelevancy. Then, after comes out hero, a firefighter in charge of burning books, lest the pesky society ever ask the question "why?"

"The Earth of the new Sun" series by Gene Wolfe is frankly, a literary masterpiece I am not smart enough to appreciate. I have never encountered an author with anywhere near the robust vocabulary of Gene Wolfe, which made it difficult for me as I am assuredly not as smart as others reading this. Nevertheless, one of the dystopian societies lived by a rule I found fascinating, they were ONLY allowed to communicate via a series of around 8 to 12 thousand quotes (I don't remember the exact number, but it was a neat concept). In this way, the community was literally incapable of dissenting against the government, having a revolution, etc.

"Sixth Column" by Robert Heinlein was published in hardcover in 1949. In it, China and Japan team up, nuke the shit out of Washington and conquer America, and begin ruling it ruthlessly. A rebellion is punished early on by the slaughter of 150k civilians. It's a book about using religion as a facade in order to overthrow a tyrannical government.

"A Scanner Darkly" by Philip K. Dick. This is a personal favorite of mine, I absolutely adore this author. Several of his books could fit on this list easily enough. In this, drugs are the nemesis of the authoritarian government. Cops at nearly every corner, at every mall, all over the place. Our hero becomes distrustful of himself and paranoid of others in this disturbing, brilliant work. More about the consequences of drug abuse than the dystopian world itself, the backdrop of it is fascinating enough to be included on my list.

How about you guys? I love this genre, and I'd like to read more before I put pen to paper and create my own.
